claims.text: Deep cryogenic treatment of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo will improve its room-temperature compressive plasticity without compromising its high yield strength.
The starting NbZrTiHfMo alloy is equiatomic.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has limited room-temperature plasticity.
The high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference in NbZrTiHfMo.
The Mo-associated electronegativity difference reduces the room-temperature plasticity of NbZrTiHfMo.
The proposed treatment consists of immersion in liquid nitrogen at approximately −196 °C followed by controlled warming.
Deep cryogenic treatment may induce phase transitions in NbZrTiHfMo.
Deep cryogenic treatment may refine the dislocation structure of NbZrTiHfMo.
Cryogenic microstructural modification may increase the number of active slip systems in NbZrTiHfMo.
Deep cryogenic treatment may relieve internal stresses associated with the high Mo content.
Cryogenic microstructural refinement will enhance dislocation mobility.
Enhanced dislocation mobility will improve plasticity while preserving high yield strength.
Deep cryogenic treatment will increase room-temperature compressive plastic strain by approximately 10–50% relative to untreated NbZrTiHfMo.
The treated alloy's compressive yield strength will remain within approximately 5% of the untreated value.
The beneficial effect will occur only within an optimized range of cryogenic temperature, dwell time, and warming rate.
Excessively severe cryogenic treatment may have adverse effects on NbZrTiHfMo.
A compositionally different Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has shown simultaneous strength and elongation improvements after deep cryogenic treatment.
The magnitude of the plasticity enhancement and the microstructural response of NbZrTiHfMo to deep cryogenic treatment are not yet characterized.
